rules.statement: Remove large or unbounded sets of rows in bounded batches of a fixed size (repeating while a batch is full), each batch in its own unit of work, instead of loading or deleting all matching rows at once.
rules.why: An unbounded removal makes one huge unit of work; bounded batches clear a long backlog in many small units of work.
rules.check: Look for prune/cleanup code that queries all matching rows without a Take/limit, or that removes everything in a single SaveChanges call.

rules.statement: Remove rows in Entity Framework stores by reading them and removing them through the change tracker, not with set-based deletes such as ExecuteDelete/ExecuteDeleteAsync.
rules.why: The EF InMemory provider does not support set-based deletes, and the change tracker gives every provider one code path.
rules.check: Flag ExecuteDelete/ExecuteDeleteAsync or raw SQL DELETE statements in store implementations.

rules.statement: A store method that removes a bounded batch takes a limit, orders the candidate rows by a stable key such as Id before applying the limit, returns the count staged, and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the limit is below one.
rules.why: A stable order makes batches deterministic, and an invalid limit is a caller error that must fail fast.
rules.check: Check batch removal methods for a missing limit guard (e.g. ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfLessThan), a missing OrderBy before Take, or no returned count.

rules.statement: Run periodic background maintenance as a hosted service that ticks on a PeriodicTimer, logs any failure of a run as a warning with a defined event id, and retries at the next tick rather than stopping the service.
rules.why: A transient failure must not stop the maintenance permanently or crash the host; the next tick runs it again.
rules.check: Look for background loops using Task.Delay or System.Threading.Timer instead of PeriodicTimer, exceptions that escape the loop, or failures swallowed without logging.

rules.statement: Design background cleanup that runs on every replica to tolerate concurrent runs without leader election: treat a concurrency conflict on saving a batch (another replica already removed the rows) as progress and continue with the next batch instead of failing.
rules.why: Leader election needs shared state, and concurrent prunes waste at most one batch.
rules.check: Check that DbUpdateConcurrencyException from a removal batch is caught and treated as a full batch, not logged as a failure or allowed to abort the run.

rules.statement: Add a database index on every timestamp column that a periodic prune query filters on.
rules.why: So the removal reads the ended rows through an index instead of scanning the table.
rules.check: When a new prune/cleanup query filters on a column (e.g. RevokedWhen, ExpiresWhen), verify the entity configuration and migration add an index on it.

rules.statement: Configure retention periods and background intervals through a public sealed options type with sensible defaults, bound from configuration and validated when the host starts (retention not negative, interval a value PeriodicTimer accepts).
rules.why: Operators set them through configuration, and invalid values must fail at startup rather than at the first tick.
rules.check: Look for hardcoded retention/interval constants, options without ValidateOnStart, or missing validation of negative or out-of-range TimeSpans.

rules.statement: Do not delete revoked or expired grants (refresh tokens, authorization codes, sessions) as soon as they end; keep them for a retention period after they end, and only count a grant as ended when it expired or was revoked (a session-type grant only when revoked).
rules.why: Ended grants are still read to detect refresh token reuse and authorization code replay; removing them early turns a reuse into an unknown token.
rules.check: Flag cleanup code that deletes grants at revocation/expiry time, prunes without subtracting a retention period, or removes non-expiring unrevoked grants or unrevoked sessions.
